SIPROTEC 5 · 7UT8x · 7SX85 · Restricted ground-fault protection (ANSI 87N) · v1.0 · 2026-10-05

87N REF Field Guide

Restricted ground-fault protection in SIPROTEC 5, step by step

This guide takes you through the restricted ground-fault protection one idea at a time. It covers what the function protects, how the relay decides, what the settings mean and how to test it. All the numbers come from one real transformer, and every test was reproduced in the SIPROTEC 5 Digital Twin.

About this guide. Written for the SIPROTEC 5 transformer differential protection devices 7UT82, 7UT85, 7UT86 and 7UT87; it can also be used for the 7SX85. Page and figure numbers refer to the 7UT8x manual V11.00 (C53000-G5040-C016-R, edition 04.2026); in the 7SX85 manual they are different. It is a practical explanation, not an official Siemens document: where it differs from the manual, the manual applies. The tests were reproduced in the SIPROTEC 5 Digital Twin; confirm the behavior with your own device and firmware version.

How to use this guide

  1. Understand the function (Parts 1 and 2). This applies to any SIPROTEC 5 transformer with a grounded star winding.
  2. Test it (Parts 3 and 4). Part 3 gives a recommended test suite of eight tests with a worked example. In Part 4 you enter your own transformer, CT and setting data, and the guide generates the injections and the expected results for you.
  3. Read records, check settings, troubleshoot (Parts 5 to 8).

All numbers in the text come from one worked example, verified in the SIPROTEC 5 Digital Twin: a 280 MVA, 230/18 kV YNd1 step-up transformer, phase CTs 2000:5, neutral CT 1200:5, Threshold 0.15, Slope 0.05, both polarity parameters = yes.

1

Understand it in five steps

1

What the REF protects

The REF watches a small zone: the star (Y) winding of the transformer, from the phase CTs at the bushings down to the CT in the neutral-to-ground connection. Its only job is to detect ground faults inside that zone, quickly and with high sensitivity.

The main transformer differential (87T) covers the whole transformer. It has trouble with ground faults close to the neutral point, where the phase currents are small, and its zero-sequence elimination makes it even less sensitive to ground faults. The REF covers that gap.

2

The rule: what goes in must come out

A YNd transformer feeds ground faults on the HV system: the delta lets zero-sequence current circulate and balance the star winding, so ground-fault current can come up through the neutral. So there are two cases:

  • Fault outside the zone (on the HV system): the same ground current comes up through the neutral CT and leaves through the phase CT. It passes both CTs, so from the zone's point of view it goes in and comes out. Nothing is missing, so the REF must not trip.
  • Fault inside the zone (in the winding): the neutral and the HV system both push current into the zone, towards the fault. The HV system contributes only if it has another grounded source; otherwise the neutral alone feeds the fault, which still trips (test 1b). Current goes in and does not come out, so the REF must trip.

Base drawing: Manual Fig. 6-98 "Basic principle of the function", p. 768. On the right it is as in the manual, with the fault inside the zone. On the left the same fault was moved past the phase CTs, outside the zone. Added on top: the REF zone (dashed), the fault current (yellow), the current at the phase CT (blue) and at the neutral CT (orange).

Remember: outside the zone, the phase and neutral currents point in opposite directions and cancel. Inside the zone, they point in the same direction and add up.

3

Putting both currents on the same scale

The two CTs have different ratios, so their secondary amperes cannot be compared directly. The relay converts both to primary amperes and then divides by the rated current of the side, IrObj = S / (√3 · V). The result is in I/IrObj, a per-unit value.

Example (280 MVA, 230 kV, IrObj = 703 A; phase CT 2000:5, neutral CT 1200:5):

Secondary currentOn the phase input (×400)On the neutral input (×240)
0.4 A160 A = 0.23 I/IrObj96 A = 0.14 I/IrObj
0.5 A200 A = 0.28 I/IrObj120 A = 0.17 I/IrObj
1 A400 A = 0.57 I/IrObj240 A = 0.34 I/IrObj
3 A1200 A = 1.71 I/IrObj720 A = 1.02 I/IrObj
5 A2000 A = 2.85 I/IrObj1200 A = 1.71 I/IrObj
10 A4000 A = 5.69 I/IrObj2400 A = 3.41 I/IrObj

Remember: compare primary amperes, never secondary amperes. In the example, 3 A on the phase input and 5 A on the neutral input are the same current (1200 A primary), but 1 A on each input is not: 400 A against 240 A.

4

The relay asks three questions

Every few milliseconds the relay works through three questions in order. Only if the first and the third answers are "yes" does it trip, and the second question can turn the third one into a "no".

Question 1 – is something wrong? The relay adds the phase and the neutral current as arrows (vectors). The result is Idiff. If Idiff is above the bar, the function picks up. Pickup alone does not trip.

Question 2 – inside or outside? The relay compares the directions of the two currents and summarizes the answer in one number, IAngle. Negative means they point the same way (inside). Positive means they point in opposite directions (outside). When the answer is "outside", the neutral current used in question 3 is reduced, down to zero for a clear outside fault.

Question 3 – is it a real ground fault? Only the neutral current can answer "yes" here, after the reduction of question 2. It is shown as I REF,operate. If it is above the bar, the relay trips. That is why phase current alone can pick up the function but can never trip it.

Why the neutral current decides the trip: the phase sum 3I0 can appear without any ground fault, for example when the phase CTs saturate unequally during a heavy external phase fault or inrush. Current in the neutral CT proves that ground current really flows through the star winding.

For the curious: the exact formulas from the manual
QuantityFormulaManual
Relay-view currents (in I/IrObj)IY* = kyx·IY
3I0* = ksx·(IA+IB+IC)		p. 768
Differential (question 1)Idiff = |IY* + 3I0*|p. 769
RestraintIrest = |IY*| + |IA*| + |IB*| + |IC*|p. 769
The barIChar = max(Threshold, Slope · Irest)Fig. 6-99
Angle quantity (question 2)IAngle = |IY* − 3I0*| − |IY* + 3I0*|p. 770
Operate quantity (question 3)angle ≤ 90°: IREF = |IY*|
angle > 90°: IREF = max(0, |IY*| − 4.05657·IAngle)		p. 771
DecisionsPickup: Idiff ≥ IChar
Operate: pickup and IREF ≥ IChar		p. 769–771

The factor 4.05657 places the tripping limit at exactly 100° between the currents when both have the same size. If the neutral current is large enough compared with the phase sum, tripping becomes possible at any angle, provided I REF,operate is still above the bar. How large depends on the settings, because the Slope also raises the bar: the manual gives a ratio IY*/3I0* above 8.9 for Threshold 0.4 / Slope 0.07, and above 13.0 for Threshold 0.2 / Slope 0.35 (Fig. 6-102, p. 772).

Note: the manual prints the first formula as "IY* = kyx · 3Iy" (p. 768). The neutral current is used once, as in the table; the Digital Twin confirms it (5 A on the neutral input gives 1.71 I/IrObj).

5

Telling the relay which way is "in"

Steps 2 and 4 depend on directions. The relay can only know whether a current flows towards the transformer if you tell it how each CT is installed and wired. That is done with one parameter per CT set:

ParameterCT setSet it to yes when…
Neutr.point in dir.of ref.obj
_:8881:116 · default yes		Phase CTs
(3-phase measuring point)		the secondary terminals that are joined into the star point belong to the CT side that faces the transformer.
Term. 1,3,5,7 in dir. of obj.
_:2311:116 · default yes		Neutral CT
(1-phase measuring point)		the CT side that faces the transformer neutral is wired to the relay's odd terminal (terminal 7). The other side faces ground.

Remember (yes / yes): if you inject the phase and the neutral input with the same angle, both entering the odd terminals, the relay sees an outside fault and stays stable. Put the neutral at 180° and it sees an inside fault and trips.

Why "same angle = outside"? In the reference connection of the manual (below), an outside fault makes both secondary currents leave the relay through the odd terminals, in the same direction. To make them cancel, SIPROTEC 5 turns the neutral current by 180° internally, in the Transformer neutral point function group. This rotation keeps compatibility with SIPROTEC 4.

The turn applies only to the current handed to the REF. The measured values and the fault record show the neutral current without it, with only the CT polarity parameter applied. In test 3 (yes / yes), both measured values read 1200 A ∠0°, yet the REF reports a fault outside the zone.

Follow the currents in the manual's reference connection

The drawing below is the manual's reference connection for yes / yes, with the currents drawn in color:

  • the yellow band is the fault current in the primary;
  • blue is the secondary loop of the phase C CT;
  • orange is the secondary loop of the neutral CT.

Switch between an outside and an inside fault and follow the numbers ① to ④.

Outside fault (the default view):

  1. ① Primary: the currents are opposite. The fault current comes up from ground through the neutral CT, through the winding, and leaves through the phase C CT towards the fault. Both CTs have P1 towards the transformer, so seen from P1 one current goes in and the other comes out.
  2. ② Wiring: S1 lands on opposite sides of the relay. On the phase CTs, S1 is joined into the star point, which connects to the even terminals (2/4/6). On the neutral CT, S1 goes to the odd terminal 7. The manual asks for exactly this: "Connect the neutral point to the 3-pole measuring points on the device side using the even-numbered terminals" (p. 768). This crossing flips the sign of one of the two currents.
  3. ③ At the relay: same direction. I3 flows in at 6 and out at 5, and I4 flows in at 8 and out at 7. Both go from the even to the odd terminal. Each loop goes out and comes back, so arrows on the long wires point both ways. The arrows that matter are the ones through the relay inputs.
  4. ④ Inside the REF: opposite again. SIPROTEC 5 turns the neutral current by 180° (p. 775–777). The two currents now point opposite ways and cancel: Idiff = |I4 − I3| = 0. Stable.

Now switch to the inside fault. The HV system now pushes current into the transformer through the phase CT, so the blue loop reverses and I3 flows from 5 to 6. The neutral loop does not change. At the terminals the two currents are now opposite, which is 180° on a test set. After the internal 180° turn they point the same way and add, and the REF trips.

Remember: a test set reproduces step ③. With yes / yes, 0° / 0° is the outside fault (test 3, stable) and 0° / 180° is the inside fault (test 4, trip). The opposition you see in the primary is real, but the crossed wiring undoes it at the terminals, and the internal 180° turn restores it.

What if the neutral CT were wired like the phases?

Suppose the neutral CT had S1 on the even terminal 8 instead of 7, the same side as the phase star point. Then step 2 would no longer flip a sign, and in step 3 the two currents would cross their inputs in opposite directions for an outside fault.

That wiring is not wrong. The relay just needs to be told: set Term. 1,3,5,7 in dir. of obj. = no for the neutral, and it compensates internally. With that setting the test angles swap: 0° / 180° becomes the outside fault and 0° / 0° the inside fault. This is the "yes for the phases, no for the neutral" case described below.

The two parameters describe the wiring; they do not fix it. Read the CT orientation and wiring first, set each parameter to match, and only then derive which test angle means "outside". Never choose the parameter from the test result.

All four combinations, and a common real case (yes for the phases, no for the neutral)
Phase CTsNeutral CTPhase and neutral at the same angleNeutral at 180°
yesyesoutside · stableinside · trip
yesnoinside · tripoutside · stable
noyesinside · tripoutside · stable
nonooutside · stableinside · trip

A common real case: yes for the phases, no for the neutral. It looks inconsistent, but it is what IEEE-style bushing CTs can give:

  • All polarity marks face away from the winding, towards the line or towards ground.
  • On every CT, the polarity lead goes to the odd relay terminal.
  • Phases: the leads joined into the star point are the non-polarity leads, on the winding side, so the phase parameter is yes.
  • Neutral: the odd terminal carries the polarity lead, on the ground side, so the neutral parameter is no.

Both answers are correct, because the two parameters ask different questions.

Golden rule: set each parameter from the real CT orientation and wiring, proven by a polarity test. Never flip a parameter just to make a test pass. A wrong parameter can make the REF fail to trip for inside faults fed from both sides and trip for outside faults.

2

Read the four values on the HMI

The relay shows the answers to the three questions as functional values. All four are in I/IrObj. HMI path: Main menu → Measurements → (function group, here the transformer side) → Function values → 87N REF (manual p. 774). In formulas this guide writes them shorter: IREF, IAngle, Idiff and Irest.

HMI lineWhat it isPlain meaningFault outsideFault inside
I REF,operateoperate quantity (question 3)neutral current that counts for tripping0= neutral current
I Angle,REFangle quantity (question 2)sign tells inside (−) or outside (+)positivenegative
I diff.differential (question 1)vector sum of phase and neutral≈ 0large
I restr.restraintsum of all current sizes; raises the bar for big through currentslarge≈ I diff. (single phase, in phase)

There is also the indication Block by direct. det. (_:305). It is the Block output of the operate-curve stage (manual Fig. 6-97): it is on while the function is picked up and the operating point (neutral current against the angle) is outside the trip region. Read it as "picked up, but held back". So the name is misleading: it does not only mean "blocked by the direction". In the Digital Twin, with every test started from zero and the LEDs reset, it came on whenever the function picked up without tripping: with no neutral current (test 2), for a fault outside the zone (test 5) and for an inside fault whose neutral current stayed below the raised bar (test 6a). In the fault record of test 8 it stayed on from pickup until Operate, about 44 ms (Part 5). If you change from an inside to an outside state without removing the current, the earlier Trip stays on and this indication does not appear.

3

Test it: a recommended test suite

The eight tests below form a recommended secondary test suite for the SIPROTEC 5 REF. Each test changes one thing and checks one behavior. Together they prove:

  • the pickup value;
  • that phase current alone cannot trip;
  • stability for faults outside the zone;
  • operation for faults inside it;
  • the slope stabilization;
  • the angle criterion.

Use the suite for commissioning, after setting changes and when you troubleshoot an unexpected trip or non-trip. The values below are those of the worked example; Part 4 generates them for your own transformer.

TestWhat it validatesPass criterion
1a / 1bPickup value, set by the neutral currentNo pickup just below the setting; trip just above it
2Phase current alone cannot tripPickup, no trip
3Stability for a fault outside the zoneNo pickup, no trip
4Operation for a fault inside the zone, and the operate timeTrip. Operate time, as a step from zero current: about 26–33 ms + output time (manual §12.3, p. 2833)
5Equal secondary amperes are not a balanced test when the CT ratios differOutside angle: pickup, no trip · inside angle: trip
6a / 6bSlope: a large phase current raises the barNeutral below the raised bar: no trip · above it: trip
7a / 7bAngle criterion90° between the currents: trip · 120°: no trip
8Fault record: polarity, and a fault that moves from outside to insideCOMTRADE shows the expected polarity; trip after the change

Before you start

  1. Read the settings from the relay itself: Threshold, Slope, both CT ratios and both polarity parameters. Check also that Operate & flt.rec. blocked (_:2) is no; with yes the REF neither trips nor writes a fault record.
  2. Keep the result clean. A current in only one phase also creates 87T differential current. Switch 87T off (Mode = off) for these tests, or judge the result only by the 87N REF 1: Operate indication in the log.
  3. Give yourself three LEDs that show only the REF: route 87N REF 1: Pickup (_:55), Operate (_:57) and Block by direct. det. (_:305). In the captures of this guide these LEDs are labelled 87N Pick Up, 87N Trip and Block by dir. det. One look then tells you how far the relay got: • all off: question 1 said no (nothing detected);
    • Pickup + Operate: the relay tripped;
    • Pickup + Block by direct. det.: question 1 said yes, but the trip was held back (no neutral current, a fault outside the zone, or a neutral current below the bar).
  4. Start every test from zero current and reset the LEDs. Otherwise an indication from the previous injection stays on and misleads you. In the worked example, going straight from the inside state to the outside state of test 5 left Trip lit and hid the Block indication.
  5. Check the angles first with test 3. The measured values must show the same primary current on the phase and on the neutral. If a channel is about 90° off, the REF trips at both the outside and the inside angle; if it is reversed (180° off), the results of tests 3 and 4 swap. Either way nothing else makes sense until it is fixed.
  6. In the Digital Twin, restart after changing CT parameters, then repeat tests 3 and 4 to confirm that the new polarity is active.

Worked example, verified in the Digital Twin

The cards run the suite on the example object: 280 MVA, 230 kV (IrObj = 703 A), phase CT 2000:5 (1 A = 400 A), neutral CT 1200:5 (1 A = 240 A), Threshold 0.15, Slope 0.05, yes / yes. Each card shows the expected values, the result measured in the SIPROTEC 5 Digital Twin and the screen capture.

Test 8

Outside, then inside, in one fault record

TRIP IN STATE 2

Record the change from an outside fault to an inside fault, to see the polarity and the timing in the COMTRADE.

Inject, as a two-state sequence
State 1 (0.5 s)I1 3 A ∠0° (1200 A) · I4 5 A ∠0° (1200 A)State 2 (≥ 0.5 s)I1 3 A ∠0° · I4 5 A ∠180°
Expect
State 1test 3: stable, no pickupState 2test 4: pickup, then tripRecordIA and IY in phase, then 180° apart

Pass criterion: no pickup in state 1, trip in state 2, and the record shows the polarity described in Part 5.

What you learn: the record confirms the manual. A fault outside shows IA and IY in phase, and a fault inside shows them 180° apart (Part 5). In this record the trip came about 44 ms after the change, with Block by direct. det. on until then. That figure belongs to this particular record (this sequence, in the Digital Twin) and is not a general operate time. Measure the operate time with test 4, as a step from zero current, and compare it with the manual (§12.3: about 33 ms at 1.5× and 27 ms at 2.5× the setting, plus the output time, at 50 Hz; 32 / 26 ms at 60 Hz).

Recommended test plan (template)

These are the tests we recommend performing on the REF: the suite of Part 3, filled in with the data entered in the calculator above. Use the table as a test plan template for commissioning, after setting changes or when troubleshooting:

  1. Check that the data above match the settings read from the relay.
  2. Copy the plan into your test report or test-set notes. The copy adds empty columns for the measured values and pass/fail.
  3. Inject each row, starting from zero current with the LEDs reset, and record what the relay shows.
  4. A test passes when the relay gives the expected result and the HMI values are close to the expected ones.

Angles are those of the test set channels, with phase A on I1 and the neutral on I4. The primary current is shown in brackets. Each value is checked with the manual's formulas before it is shown.

TestPurposeI1 phase AI4 neutralExpected: I REF,op · I Angle · I diff. · I restr. · barExpected result
How the injections are chosen

kp and kn are the primary amperes per secondary ampere of the phase and neutral CTs. In is the CT secondary rating (1 A or 5 A). Currents are rounded to "easy" values: phase currents and the pairs of tests 3 and 4 to multiples of In/5 where possible, otherwise In/100; the neutral currents of tests 1 and 6 to multiples of In/100. Where a margin is too small, the current is moved step by step until it is met. Every row is then checked with the manual's formulas, and a row is marked ⚠ if it does not give the result the test is meant to show, or if it needs more than 4 × In.

TestRule
1a / 1bNeutral only. The pickup in neutral amperes is Threshold × IrObj / kn. Inject a little below it, rounded down (1a, typically 85–95 %), and a little above it, rounded up until it trips (1b, typically 105–115 %).
2Phase only, 20 % of In (raised if needed so that Idiff is at least twice the Threshold).
3 / 4The same primary current in both CTs, at least IrObj: Iphase × kp = Ineutral × kn, with the smallest pair of easy values. Neutral at the outside angle (3) or the inside angle (4).
5The same secondary current on both inputs, 20 % of In (raised until 5a clearly picks up and 5b clearly trips), at the outside angle and then at the inside angle. Not applicable when kp = kn, and not meaningful when the ratios are so far apart that 5b cannot trip or 5a trips.
6a / 6bA phase current that makes Irest about twice the knee (Threshold / Slope), so the bar rises. Neutral at the inside angle: just above the Threshold (6a, which must stay under the raised bar), then about 15 % above the raised bar (6b). Skipped when Slope = 0, or when the Slope is so steep that 6b would need an impractical neutral current.
7a / 7bThe currents of test 3, with the neutral turned 90° (7a) and 120° (7b) away from the inside angle.
8A two-state sequence: test 3 for 0.5 s, then test 4 for at least 0.5 s. Record the COMTRADE. The operate time is measured separately, with test 4 as a step from zero current.
5

Read the fault record (COMTRADE)

One detail surprises almost everybody the first time: in the fault record, the neutral current is drawn turned by 180° compared with the relay's own view. The manual says so in two places:

"Consider that the neutral-point current (IY) detected using the 1-phase measuring point is displayed as positive in the fault record and in the DIGSI 5 Test Suite if the current flows from the protected object to ground."Manual §6.5.3, p. 768
"The current Iy measured at the neutral point is turned by 180° in the fault record (COMTRADE). […] To be compatible with SIPROTEC 4 […] a rotation of the polarity (phase rotation by 180°) is also carried out in the Transformer neutral point function group."Manual §6.5.4, p. 775

Remember: in the COMTRADE, a fault outside shows IA and IY in phase, and a fault inside shows them 180° apart. That is the opposite of the arrows in step 2, and it is normal. (This holds for a single-phase test injection or a phase-A ground fault. In general, compare IY with 3I0, the sum of the three phase currents.)

Record values at selected instants (table view)
t (ms)I diff.I REF,operateI Angle,REFPickupBlock by direct. det.Operate

Because the record shows the currents with the CT polarity parameters applied, the first energization of the transformer from the star side is a useful plausibility check of the polarity. The zero-sequence part of the inrush current flows through the zone, like an outside fault. In the record you should see IY in phase with 3I0 (the sum IA + IB + IC, not IA alone), with I Angle positive and I REF,operate = 0. Three limits: energizing from the delta side gives no zero-sequence current on the star side; the zero-sequence inrush can be small and offset; and a stable REF does not pick up, so the record must be triggered by something else (87T pickup, the inrush detection or a manual trigger).

6

The settings, explained

Threshold: the height of the bar

The Threshold is set in I/IrObj of the side where the function sits, here the 230 kV side (703 A). The relay does not let you go below 5 % of the largest CT primary current used by the function:

Lower limit = max{ 0.05 ; 0.05 × ICT,prim,max / IrObj }, where ICT,prim,max is the largest primary rating of the CTs used by the REF (manual p. 774).

Example: max{0.05 ; 0.05 × 2000 A / 703 A} = 0.142, so the first setting step above it is 0.15. A value such as 0.10 is rejected by DIGSI. In amperes: 0.15 × 703 A = 105 A primary, or 0.44 A on the neutral input. That is the smallest neutral current that trips; tests 1a and 1b check it.

0.15 is the choice of the worked example, the most sensitive value its CTs allow. The manual recommends 0.20 I/IrObj, which is also the default, and notes that the neutral current of a fault near the neutral point is large enough, so there is no need to set the Threshold sensitive (p. 779, 786).

Slope: raising the bar for big through faults

During a heavy fault outside the zone, the CTs may not reproduce the current perfectly, and a false differential current could appear. The slope raises the bar in proportion to the total current (Irest):

IChar = max( Threshold ; Slope × Irest ). The bar stays at the Threshold until Irest = Threshold / Slope (the knee), then rises.

How to choose the Slope (manual p. 780): the bar should not rise below rated load. At rated load Irest = |IA| + |IB| + |IC| = 3 (one measuring point, or several on the outgoing side; use 6 with two measuring points on the supply side). So the slope line goes through the origin and crosses the Threshold at 3: Slope = Threshold / 3. Example: 0.15 / 3 = 0.05; with the recommended 0.20 it gives 0.07, the default.

SettingValueWhy
Mode (_:1)onfunction active (default off)
Operate & flt.rec. blocked (_:2)nodefault; yes would suppress the trip and the fault record
Threshold (_:103)0.15 I/IrObjlowest step above the limit of 0.142 (100 A primary); 0.15 = 105 A. Manual recommendation and default: 0.20
Slope (_:105)0.050.15 / 3; the bar starts to rise above rated load (default 0.07)
Operate delay (_:109)0.00 sdefault; REF is a unit protection and needs no grading
7

Prove the installation in the field

A secondary test proves the relay logic and the settings. It cannot prove how the CTs are installed and wired. The manual (§11.8, p. 2755) recommends:

  1. Polarity test of the CTs, making sure the positive direction (towards the protected object) is respected. For the phase CTs, the CT star point points to the protected object.
  2. Pickup check by feeding a current into the neutral CT circuit.
  3. Stability check by passing a primary current through the neutral CT and one phase CT, as a through current. This is possible only where there are no bushing CTs. The REF must not trip.
  4. Generator step-up transformers: use the generator as the source. During a shutdown, install an external single-phase short circuit, set the REF to its lowest setting value, then excite the generator to supply a minimum current, below the permissible negative-sequence current. Only if a larger test current is needed, keep the test short (a few seconds). Restore the primary plant and the settings afterwards.
  5. Smaller transformers (low rated currents): the test can use an external supply instead (the "400 V method"), with the REF set to its minimum Threshold.
CheckWhat it provesWhat you should see
CT ratio and polarity test, injecting through the winding, polarity checked at the relay terminalsratio, polarity and wiring of phase and neutral CTsagrees with the two polarity parameters (step 5)
Fault record at the first energization from the star sideplausibility of the polarity under real conditions (inrush zero-sequence = through current)COMTRADE: IY in phase with 3I0 · I Angle > 0 · I REF,operate = 0 (the record needs a trigger, see Part 5)
GSU short-circuit test with the generatorCTs, wiring, settings and stability (not the trip circuit)no trip; IY in phase with 3I0 in the record

A note on §11.8. The same page also says that the side of the neutral CT connected to terminal A7 must be in the direction of ground. Read literally, this seems to contradict the reference connection of Fig. 6-109 (p. 778), where the neutral CT side that faces the transformer neutral goes to the odd terminal 7 and the parameter must be yes. This guide follows Fig. 6-109 and p. 778, and the Digital Twin behaves accordingly. Whatever the drawing says, set Term. 1,3,5,7 in dir. of obj. from the real wiring and confirm it with tests 3 and 4.

Watch out: the 87T load check does not prove the neutral CT. Load current has no zero-sequence component, so a reversed neutral CT stays hidden until a ground fault or an energization record shows it.

8

Troubleshooting

We injected the same current at 0° into the phase and neutral inputs and the REF did not trip.

With yes / yes that injection is a fault outside the zone (step 5), so not tripping is the correct answer. Try 1 A ∠0° on I1 and 1 A ∠0° on I4 in the calculator:

  • Question 1: Idiff = 0.23, above 0.15, so it picks up. 1 A against 1 A is not the same primary current (400 A against 240 A), so the currents do not cancel completely.
  • Question 2: the currents are opposite, so IAngle = +0.68 and the neutral current is reduced to 0.
  • Question 3: I REF,operate = 0, so there is no trip.

Put the neutral at 180° and the same currents trip: I REF,operate = 0.34. This is test 5 of Part 3.

The REF picked up but did not trip.

Question 1 was "yes" but question 3 was "no". Three typical reasons:

  • There is no neutral current (test 2).
  • The fault is outside, so question 2 reduces the neutral current to zero (test 5).
  • The neutral current is below the bar, which a large through current has raised (test 6).
Why is I diff. equal to I restr. in some tests?

Idiff adds the currents as arrows. Irest adds only their sizes. When the relay sees the two currents pointing exactly the same way (a clean inside fault), both sums give the same number. Example from test 4: 1.707 + 1.707 = 3.41 for both. With any angle between the currents, Idiff becomes smaller than Irest.

Why can't the Threshold be 0.10? Is it referred to the HV side?

Yes, it is referred to the rated current of the side whose function group contains the REF, here 230 kV, 703 A. The lower limit is 5 % of the largest CT primary current (2000 A), which gives 0.142. DIGSI rejects anything lower (Part 6).

The characteristic in DIGSI shows "I diff.", but the trip uses I REF,operate. Why?

Both use the same bar. Idiff decides the pickup (question 1). The neutral current decides the trip (question 3), because only the neutral CT proves that ground current really flows in the star winding. A false 3I0 can appear when the phase CTs saturate unequally, for example during a heavy external fault or inrush. (Inrush can also contain real zero-sequence current, but that also flows through the neutral CT, as a through current.)

The relay tripped although I REF,operate was 0.

Another function tripped, normally 87T: a current in one phase of one side looks like a differential current to 87T. Check the log to see which function issued Operate, and switch 87T off during REF tests.

In the COMTRADE the neutral current looks reversed.

That is by design (Part 5). In the record, a fault outside shows IA and IY in phase, and a fault inside shows them 180° apart. This holds for a single-phase injection; in general compare IY with 3I0, the sum of the phase currents.

The REF trips at both 0° and 180°.

Check the measured angles first. In one Digital Twin session, the neutral channel arrived about 90° away from the phase channel. With the currents at 90°, question 2 cannot decide (IAngle ≈ 0), so the relay tripped in both cases. Fix the channel before testing anything else.

I changed a polarity parameter, but the Digital Twin still behaves the old way.

Restart the Digital Twin after changing CT parameters, then repeat tests 3 and 4 to confirm the new convention. In one session the twin kept the old polarity until it was restarted: test 5 (1 A / 1 A at 0°) tripped, because the relay was still treating it as an inside fault. After the restart the same injection gave the expected pickup without trip.

The LEDs stay on after a test.

The LEDs are latched. Reset them before every injection, and confirm the result in the log.
